subject: Orthopedics
title: Acute Compartment Syndrome: The Time-Critical Limb
preview: Rising pressure within a noncompliant compartment can compromise perfusion and nerves before pulses disappear.

sections.title: Recognition
points: Trauma, fractures, reperfusion and tight casts or dressings are common contexts.
Serial examination matters when symptoms evolve after an initially reassuring assessment.

sections.title: Physiologic logic
points: Pressure reduces local capillary perfusion and threatens ischemic muscle and nerves.
Objective pressure measurements may assist in selected difficult assessments, but do not replace clinical urgency.

sections.title: Exam trap
points: Palpable distal pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome.
Do not wait for paralysis or pulselessness in a patient with strong early clinical warning signs.

quickRevision: Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are classic early warning features.
Sensory disturbance and tense compartments increase concern; pulses may remain present until late.
Urgent surgical assessment and removal of external constriction are crucial when suspected.

quiz.question: Which finding is a warning for acute compartment syndrome?
options: Normal painless passive movement as a universal rule-out
quiz.explanation: Severe pain out of proportion, particularly on passive stretch, is an early sign of compartment syndrome; pulses can remain present.
